## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91033.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91033.3.sa1)

The formation of long-term memory representations requires the continuous updating of ongoing representations. Various studies have shown that the left angular gyrus (AG) may support this cognitive operation. However, this study demonstrates that this brain region plays a causal role in the formation of long-term memory representations, affecting both the neural and behavioural measures of information binding.

A significant strength of this work is that it is the first one to test the hypothesis that the left angular gyrus has a causal role in the reconfiguration and binding of long-term memory representations by comparing when insights are primarily derived from direct observation versus imagination. Consequently, the results from this manuscript have the potential to be informative for all areas of cognitive research, including basic perception, language cognition and memory.

Furthermore, this study presents a comprehensive set of measurements on the same individuals, encompassing various task-related behavioural measures, EEG data, and questionnaire responses.

A weakness of the manuscript is the use of different groups of participants for the key TMS intervention.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.91033.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.91033.3.sa2)

The authors have done a fine job of updating the manuscript and it is substantially improved. In particular, the paragraphs towards the end of the Introduction and Discussion are vastly improved. The last paragraph of the Introduction now clearly explicates the hypotheses (save one minor point of confusion). The limitations section of the Discussion is also very helpful and fair. However, there are still areas where claims need to be tempered.

Major criticisms

• The results still do not lead to the conclusion that the angular gyrus is causally involved in insight-driven memory configuration. Although the authors do state that other regions such as the hippocampus may have contributed to the pattern of results, there is still no evidence of target engagement or a link between target engagement and the behavioral results. Thus, while the results support that cTBS to the angular gyrus affects insight-driven memory configuration, it is a strong overstep to say that the angular gyrus is causally involved in insight-driven memory reconfiguration. In particular, this applies to both the title and the last line of the Abstract. In relation to this, have the authors conducted any target engagement analyses? It seems like a good starting point would be to identify the censor closest to the stimulation site in each individual, Hjorth transforms the signal of that sensor by subtracting the average of the surrounding sensors to increase signal localization, and then measure the effects of stimulation on theta power. Presumably, we would expect that cTBS would decrease theta power relative to sham stimulation. Although this isn't the only type of analysis that could at least partially confirm target engagement, there needs to be some sort of formal analysis to maintain the claims of the title and last line of the Abstract.

• The authors removed the mentions of "inhibitory stimulation" from the manuscript to their credit, but a rigorous and fair treatment of the effects of cTBS is still lacking, and it is still unclear why cTBS to the angular gyrus would cause an inhibitory effect in the first place. The authors state that

"Previous evidence has demonstrated the inhibitory effect of cTBS on the targeted brain region under stimulation (Huang et al., 2005; Jannati et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the effects of cTBS appear to vary based on the targeted region, with cTBS to parietal regions demonstrating the capability to enhance hippocampal connectivity (Hermiller et al., 2019, 2020)."

The inhibitory effects of motor cortex cTBS s on corticospinal excitability in nine subjects from the Huang paper and the Jannati review (not a primary source) do not constitute sufficient evidence to hypothesize an inhibitory effect on insight-driven memory reconfiguration. The second sentence provides much more sufficient evidence that parietal stimulation should have some sort of a facilitatory effect, but this is simply glossed over without an explanation of why cTBS to the parietal cortex should inhibit insight-driven memory reconfiguration. Pilot data showing such inhibitory effects or a body of evidence showing inhibitory effects of angular gyrus stimulation on closely-related areas of cognition would have given reason to believe this. However, without these, an a priori assumption that parietal cTBS would be inhibitory seems highly debatable and paints the results as provisional, rather than confirmatory"

results.result: The study employed a rigorous double-blind, preregistered design with 65 participants randomly assigned to cTBS or sham groups. Groups were well-matched on demographic and psychological variables, participants were blind to condition assignment, and TMS did not affect mood or attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C68-C70 establish strong methodological rigor through preregistration (C27), adequate sample size (C28), matched groups on control variables (C29), successful blinding (C68), and absence of non-specific TMS effects on mood/attention (C69-C70). These collectively support the validity of the experimental design.

results.result: All participants successfully gained insight into which events were linked, as demonstrated by increased belongingness ratings for linked events, closer spatial arrangement in the multi-arrangements task, and near-ceiling forced-choice recognition. Critically, there were no group differences on these measures, indicating that cTBS to the angular gyrus did not impair the process of gaining insight itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 provide converging evidence from multiple behavioral measures (belongingness ratings, multi-arrangements task, forced-choice recognition) that all participants gained insight successfully and that groups did not differ. The statistical analyses support these claims with appropriate tests and effect sizes. The inference that the angular gyrus is not critical for gaining insight (C37) is well-supported by the absence of group differences.

results.result: cTBS to the left angular gyrus selectively reduced the memory advantage for linked events during free recall. While linked events were generally recalled in more detail than non-linked events across groups, the cTBS group showed significantly fewer recalled details for linked events compared to sham, with no difference for non-linked events. All participants showed better memory for central versus peripheral details when recalling linked events.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 demonstrate the primary behavioral effect of cTBS on memory integration. The group × link interaction (C39) with appropriate post-hoc tests (C40-C41) provides strong statistical evidence. The effect is specific to linked events, supporting the causal role of the angular gyrus in memory integration. The detail analysis (C42) adds depth to the characterization of memory effects.

results.result: cTBS to the angular gyrus significantly reduced recall of the linking events themselves, with this effect appearing more pronounced for events linked via imagination compared to observation, though the interaction was not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is well-supported by statistical analysis showing reduced recall of linking events after cTBS. Claim C44 notes a pattern suggesting stronger effects for imagination-based linking, but appropriately acknowledges the non-significant interaction. The claims are appropriately cautious given the statistical evidence.

results.result: Electric field modeling revealed that the behavioral effects of cTBS were dependent on stimulation strength. Stronger electric field induction in the angular gyrus significantly reduced the memory boost for linked events and impaired recall of linking events, while weak stimulation showed no such effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 provide important validation that the observed effects are dose-dependent and specifically related to angular gyrus stimulation strength. The electric field modeling approach (described in C113) and median-split analysis with appropriate statistical tests support these claims. This strengthens the causal interpretation of the findings.

results.result: For events linked via imagination, the sham group showed increased neural representational similarity in the theta band from pre- to post-insight, while the cTBS group showed no increase and even a trend toward decreased similarity. Lower changes in representational similarity were associated with reduced recall of linking events.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 demonstrate the neural mechanism underlying the behavioral effects for imagination-based linking. The RSA analysis shows a clear group × time interaction with appropriate follow-up tests. The brain-behavior correlation (C49) strengthens the interpretation that neural pattern reconfiguration is functionally relevant for memory. The statistical analyses are appropriate and effect sizes are reported.

results.result: For events linked via observation, the sham group showed decreased neural representational similarity while the cTBS group showed increased similarity. However, these effects should be interpreted with caution as they appeared to be driven at least in part by pre-existing group differences before insight was gained.
results.evaluation: While claims C50-C51 report statistically significant effects, claim C52 appropriately raises concerns about interpretation due to baseline differences. This caveat is critical and suggests these observation-based findings may not reflect true effects of the manipulation. The authors' caution is warranted, making the interpretation of these specific results uncertain.

results.result: For non-linked events in the imagination condition, the cTBS group showed increased neural similarity from pre- to post-insight (resembling the pattern seen for linked events in the sham group), while the sham group showed no representational changes. This suggests that cTBS to the angular gyrus interfered with efficient pruning of events not part of the integrated narrative.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 reveal an important secondary effect: cTBS impaired the ability to distinguish linked from non-linked events at the neural level. The pattern comparison across conditions (C55) and the inference about failed narrative pruning (C56) are well-supported by the data. This adds important mechanistic insight into how the angular gyrus contributes to memory organization.

results.result: For non-linked events in the observation condition, the sham group showed no representational change while the cTBS group showed decreased neural similarity. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution as differences appeared to be present before insight was gained.
results.evaluation: Similar to the linked events in the observation condition, claims C57-C58 report significant effects but C65 appropriately cautions against interpretation due to pre-existing differences. The authors' acknowledgment of this limitation is appropriate and prevents overinterpretation of potentially spurious findings.

results.result: For events linked via imagination, cTBS to the angular gyrus decreased functional connectivity in the theta band between centro-temporal and frontal regions, while the sham group showed no change. Higher coherence between these regions was associated with better recall of details for imagination-linked events, suggesting that reduced connectivity impaired subsequent memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide converging neural evidence for the mechanism of cTBS effects on imagination-based memory integration. The coherence analysis complements the RSA findings, showing disrupted long-range connectivity. The brain-behavior correlation (C61-C62) strengthens the functional interpretation. Statistical analyses are appropriate with cluster-based permutation testing.

results.result: For events linked via observation, the sham group showed decreased functional connectivity between centro-temporal and frontal regions while the cTBS group showed increased connectivity. However, these differences appeared to be present before insight was gained and should be interpreted with caution.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 report statistically significant effects, but C65 appropriately raises concerns about pre-existing differences. This pattern of cautionary interpretation for observation-based findings is consistent with the RSA results and suggests these effects may not reflect true consequences of the manipulation.

results.result: No significant connectivity changes were found for non-linked events, indicating that the reported connectivity changes were specific to linked events.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 establish the specificity of the connectivity effects to linked events. This control analysis strengthens the interpretation that the observed connectivity changes are specifically related to memory integration processes rather than general effects of the task or stimulation.

results.result: The study demonstrates a causal role of the left angular gyrus in insight-driven memory reconfiguration. cTBS to the angular gyrus decreased memory for linking events, reduced the memory advantage for linked events, reduced centro-temporal coupling with frontal regions, abolished insight-induced neural representational changes for imagination-linked events, and impaired the separation of linked from non-linked events in memory.
results.evaluation: This set of claims represents the main conclusion of the study. The causal interpretation (C7, C75-C76) is well-supported by converging evidence from behavioral (C2-C3), neural representational (C5-C6), and connectivity (C4) measures. The mechanistic interpretations (C77, C85-C86, C90, C99-C100) are appropriately grounded in the data. The use of TMS provides causal evidence beyond correlational neuroimaging studies.

results.result: Participants adhered well to task instructions, reporting high levels of imagination quality and understanding for imagination and observation conditions respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by self-report data showing participants followed instructions appropriately. This validates that the manipulation of insight mode (imagination vs. observation) was successful and that participants engaged with the task as intended.

results.result: The introduction establishes the theoretical background: the angular gyrus is involved in episodic memory and imagination, has connections to the hippocampus and other regions, and may act as a dynamic buffer for spatiotemporal representations. Previous research has shown insight-driven memory reconfigurations and the role of the hippocampus, but understanding of cortical contributions beyond the hippocampus remains limited, and existing data are mainly correlational.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the rationale for the study through citations to prior literature. The characterization of the angular gyrus's functions (C1, C18-C26) and the gap in knowledge (C15-C17) are appropriately supported by citations. This provides strong justification for investigating the causal role of the angular gyrus.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within prior literature on episodic memory organization, angular gyrus connectivity, theta oscillations, and associative memory. The angular gyrus is characterized as a major connector hub with extensive connections to multiple brain regions including the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, striatum, and sensory-motor areas.
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately situate the findings within the broader literature through citations. The characterization of the angular gyrus as a connector hub (C91-C95) and the discussion of relevant prior findings (C73-C74, C78-C79, C83, C87, C96-C98, C106, C109-C110) provide important context for interpreting the results.

results.result: The authors propose several mechanistic interpretations: cTBS may have disrupted reactivation and maintenance of separate events during linking, prevented full access to detailed memory representations, and differentially affected imagination versus observation due to the angular gyrus's role in imaginative processes. The ventral location of the stimulation site may explain stronger effects on imagination-based insight due to stronger hippocampal connectivity.
results.evaluation: These claims (C80-C82, C84, C88-C89, C101-C105, C107-C108, C112) represent speculative mechanistic interpretations. While they are plausible and grounded in theory, they go beyond what the data directly demonstrate. The authors appropriately use cautious language ("may have," "may be," "it may be speculated"), but these remain hypotheses requiring further testing.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including that it detected impaired (rather than enhanced) associative memory following cTBS, the limited spatial resolution of TMS for targeting specific angular gyrus subregions, and suggests potential clinical applications for integrating fragmented memories in disorders like PTSD.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 appropriately notes a discrepancy with some prior studies. Claim C113 acknowledges an important methodological limitation regarding TMS spatial precision. Claim C114 is appropriately speculative about potential applications. These demonstrate appropriate scientific caution and acknowledgment of limitations.

results.result: cTBS to the angular gyrus reduced memory for linked events relative to non-linked events. The cTBS group showed significantly lower recall of details for linked events compared to the sham group, while there was no significant difference for non-linked events.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the 'clear-cut behavioral results' and that the study provides 'solid evidence' for the angular gyrus playing a role in insight-based memory updating. However, they emphasize that 'evidence for the strong claim of a causal contribution of the angular gyrus in particular – apart from other connected regions, including the hippocampus – is not conclusive.' The lack of target engagement analyses and the possibility that effects arise from interconnected regions rather than the angular gyrus itself undermines the causal interpretation.
